title: Ashbacker Radio Corp. v. FCC (1945)
summary: When two applications for a broadcast facility are mutually exclusive, the Commission may not grant one without a hearing and then offer the loser a hearing, because that hearing would be empty.
notes:
Key line: "We only hold that where two bona fide applications are mutually exclusive the grant of one without a hearing to both deprives the loser of the opportunity which Congress chose to give him." (Douglas, J.)

Citation: 326 U.S. 327 (1945).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was Ashbacker Radio Corporation, licensee of station WKBZ in Muskegon, Michigan, which wanted to move its station to a new frequency. The respondent was the Federal Communications Commission, which had granted a competing application filed by the Fetzer Broadcasting Company for a new station in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on the same frequency. Fetzer was not a party before the Supreme Court. The United States supported the Commission. The dispute was over procedure under section 309(a) of the Communications Act of 1934, which lets the Commission grant an application upon examination if the public interest would be served and requires a hearing before an application is denied.
sections.Material Facts: In March 1944 Fetzer Broadcasting Company applied for a construction permit for a new station at Grand Rapids operating on 1230 kilocycles with 250 watts of power, unlimited time. In May 1944, before the Fetzer application was acted on, Ashbacker applied to change WKBZ in Muskegon from 1490 kilocycles to 1230 kilocycles. The Commission found that simultaneous operation on 1230 kilocycles at Grand Rapids and Muskegon would cause intolerable interference to both and declared the two applications actually exclusive. On June 27, 1944, the Commission granted the Fetzer application without a hearing and, the same day, set Ashbacker's application for hearing. One issue for that hearing was the interference Ashbacker's station would cause to Fetzer's. The Commission denied Ashbacker's petition for a hearing and rehearing on the Fetzer grant, saying the later hearing would give Ashbacker ample opportunity to show its proposal better served the public interest.
sections.Procedural History: Ashbacker appealed the grant of the Fetzer construction permit to the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia under section 402(b)(2) of the Act, claiming to be a person aggrieved or adversely affected by the Commission's decision. The Commission moved to dismiss for want of jurisdiction. The court of appeals granted the motion without opinion. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 325 U.S. 846, because of the importance of the question. The case was argued on November 13, 1945, and decided on December 3, 1945. The Court reversed. Justices Black and Jackson took no part in the consideration or decision of the case.
sections.Issue: Whether an applicant for a construction permit under the Communications Act receives the hearing to which section 309(a) entitles it when the Commission, having before it two mutually exclusive applications, grants one without a hearing and sets the other for a later hearing. Put differently, the question was whether the power to grant a license on a finding of public interest, convenience or necessity supports granting one of two exclusive applications without hearing the other, or whether the grant effectively denies the second applicant without the statutory hearing.
sections.Holding: The Court held that where two bona fide applications are mutually exclusive, the grant of one without a hearing on both deprives the loser of the opportunity for a hearing that Congress chose to give it. Although Ashbacker's statutory right to a hearing had been preserved in form, the grant to Fetzer had substantially nullified it as a practical matter. The dismissal of the appeal was reversed. The Court decided only a matter of procedure and expressed no view on the merits of either application or on which procedure would be wiser policy.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Douglas explained that section 309(a) does two things: it lets the Commission grant licenses without a hearing, and it gives applicants a right to a hearing before their applications are denied. If the grant of one exclusive application effectively precludes the other, the statutory right to a hearing becomes an empty thing. The Commission's own hearing notice showed the problem, because it listed as an issue the interference Ashbacker's proposal would cause to Fetzer's station, and the Commission had already found that simultaneous operation would produce intolerable interference. Ashbacker therefore carried a burden that could not be met, and its hearing became in substance a rehearing on the grant of its competitor's license. Because the Fetzer grant was not conditional and a stay was denied, Ashbacker stood in the position of a newcomer trying to displace an established licensee, a showing the Commission itself had described as difficult. Nothing in the record suggested a finding that the public interest was so urgent as to preclude the delay of a hearing. Ashbacker had standing under Sanders Radio Station and National Broadcasting Co., because it was at least as adversely affected as the protestants in those cases. Whether comparative hearings were wise policy was for Congress, not the Court.

topics.lrs-o-third-party-hearings: Mutually exclusive applications required comparative consideration so the first grant would not empty the second applicant’s statutory hearing of practical value.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 1, with Justices Black and Jackson not participating. Justice Frankfurter dissented. He argued that courts should not assume the familiar is the necessary and should not demand that agencies follow conventional judicial procedures when Congress has not required them; Congress moved outside the framework of protected property rights in broadcasting, and the Commission had the authority to decide whether to grant one application without a public hearing while giving the other applicant its hearing later, since the later hearing could still lead to modification of the earlier grant.
